newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark says lost China vote a victory for rights.
newsitem.headline: Denmark says lost China vote a victory for rights.

text.p: Denmark said on Wednesday that it had succeeded in focusing international attention on Chinese human rights despite the failure of its proposed U.N. resolution criticising Beijing.

Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen told the daily Jyllands-Posten that the motion at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva had prompted "serious debate" in Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden and elsewhere.

"Therefore it is not the result of the vote in Geneva that counts. France's blockade of a joint EU position has in fact focused attention on the issue to an extent that would otherwise not have been the case," he said.
Denmark, with U.S. support, tabled the motion at the commission on Tuesday, after France and Germany backed away from supporting the traditional European Union resolution.
A blocking motion by China prevented the Western resolution coming to a vote. The Chinese counter-offensive had a majority of 27 against 17 with nine states, including Russia, abstaining.

China has warned that Denmark will suffer politically and economically for leading the rights motion. So far Beijing has postponed planned visits by the Danish ministers of justice and social affairs.
The debate was preceded by a week of intensive diplomatic lobbying on both sides and a Chinese pledge to sign the U.N. International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.

"Some of the countries that made up their minds at the last minute had had the Chinese foreign ministry on the phone once an hour. There was a real battle for votes," Danish delegation head Tyge Lehmann told Jyllands-Posten.
The paper said that Beijing told Uruguay, for example, that it would cancel a major order for woollen products if Montevideo supported the Danish motion.
Like Petersen, Lehmann said that the political impact of the attempted resolution went far beyond the Geneva meeting-room.
"I think that it was fantastically successful in keeping China on the world agenda," he told Danish radio.
As well as driving debate on the issue, Denmark can also bask in the warm glow of U.S. approval.
"We congratulate the government of Denmark for sponsoring the resolution and the others who supported it," U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Tuesday.
Danish newspapers have said that Denmark sponsored the motion at Washington's request, but U.S. diplomats in Copenhagen and Petersen refuse to comment.
The United States on Tuesday said it was postponing punitive action against European Union meat imports, averting a potential trade war which would have mainly hit Danish pork products.

The effect on Danish trade with China remains to be seen. Denmark's sales to China -- mainly machinery and chemical products -- total only around one billion crowns ($152 million) out of total exports of 283.5 billion in 1996.
But several of Denmark's leading companies have extensive investments within in China and the Confederation of Danish Industries has said that it fears that they may be hurt.
A May trip by Education Minister Ole Vig Jensen to China is to go ahead, as is a private visit in July by Danish Prince Joachim and Princess Alexandra.

The prince, younger son of Danish Queen Margrethe, and his Hong Kong-born wife are to attend ceremonies on July 1 formally marking the handover of the British territory to Beijing, and will then tour China.
($ = 6.578 Danish Crowns)
